title: Black-box model classification under the discriminative factorization
claim: Query sets that probe the distinguishing axis give consistently lower classification error than orthogonal ones, across query budgets and model counts.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right: stacked embedding scatters, then two line plots
description: Three-panel figure. Panel (a) has two stacked 2-D MDS scatter plots, titled 'Signal queries, m=5' (top) and 'Orthogonal queries, m=5' (bottom). Each dot is a model: blue circles are Class 0 and orange squares are Class 1. In the signal plot the two classes separate into left and right clusters. In the orthogonal plot they overlap in a few tight clusters. Panel (b) is a line plot of mean error against the number of queries m on a log axis, with n=50. Panel (c) is a line plot of mean error against the number of models n, with m=5. Both line plots show three curves: Signal (solid blue, lowest error), Uniform (dotted green, in the middle) and Orthogonal (dashed orange, highest error). All curves decline as m or n increases. A faint dotted line at 0.5 marks chance level. The eye goes first to the scatter plots, then to the ordered curves.
caption: Classification of models by the presence of particular fine-tuning data. An oracle knows which queries probe the axis that distinguishes the two classes (Signal) and which do not (Orthogonal). (a) Two-dimensional MDS embeddings using $m = 5$ signal queries (top) and orthogonal queries (bottom). Each dot is a model. (b) Classification error as a function of query budget $m$ with $ n = 50 $ for signal, orthogonal, and uniform query sets. (c) Classification error as a function of number of models with $ m = 5 $ for the same query sets. The relative discriminative quality of the three query sets is stable across $ m $ and $ n $. Reported errors are the average of 500 different random samples.
abstract: Access to modern generative systems is often restricted to querying an API (the ``black-box'' setting) and many properties of the system are unknown to the user at inference time. Recent work has shown that low-dimensional representations of models based on the relationship of their embedded responses to a set of queries are useful for inferring model-level properties. However, the quality of these representations is highly sensitive to the query set. We introduce the \emph{discriminative factorization} to distinguish between high- and low-quality query sets in the context of black-box model-level classification. Under this framework, the probability of chance-level classification is bounded by a term that decays exponentially in the query budget. On three auditing tasks, estimated factorization parameters predict the empirical performance decay rate. We conclude by showing that query sets selected using the estimated factorization reproduce the empirical ordering of oracle query sets.
